summary: COSMOSIS is an interactive 3D space exploration and flight academy that tells the story of NASA’s abandoned hardware, from lunar landers and rovers on the Moon to Mars rovers and deep-space probes like Voyager. Instead of reading about equipment that has been left behind, students fly to it, explore it in 3D, and learn what each machine was built to do, what science it made possible, and what condition it’s in today. Built for school-age space enthusiasts, COSMOSIS turns “discarded” hardware into stories of discovery, showing that these machines are abandoned but not forgotten.
details:
COSMOSIS is an interactive 3D “student space academy” that tells the stories of NASA’s left-behind hardware, built for school-age space enthusiasts. Learners fly through a 3D solar system and open the Command Deck, which holds 10 worlds, a 3D spacecraft hangar, 6 mission chronicles, and 4 physics labs.

How it works: Clicking a world zooms in on its story, live telemetry, and a gravity simulator (for example, your weight on Mars). The Mission Chronicles are narrated, choice-driven stories about real hardware: the Apollo 11 Eagle lunar module, the Opportunity rover, whose 90-day mission lasted 5,352 sols, and Voyager 1 with its Golden Record. Learners then try the science themselves with a lunar-lander simulator across the Moon, Mars, and Europa, and an orbital-mechanics lab based on Newton’s cannonball. XP, levels, and mission patches keep students engaged.

Benefits and impact: It turns “discarded” machines into stories of discovery and connects each one to the physics behind it. It is free, runs in the browser, and needs no install or login.

Creativity: Instead of a static timeline, learners play through the decisions behind each mission, such as the Apollo 1202 alarm.

Tools: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Three.js for 3D, hosted on Vercel

Factors considered: Age-appropriate language, accuracy of mission facts, accessibility (keyboard controls, optional sound), and keeping it fun enough to learn from.
